title: The cry
hook: Rama's voice, faked; Sita sends Lakshmana

segments.voice: Yesterday: Maricha, the golden deer, and Rama chasing it deep into the forest. Wanting is the hook. Deep in the trees, Rama finally draws his bow.

The arrow hits. The golden deer falls, and as it dies, it changes. The gold drains away, and there on the ground is Maricha, a huge rakshasa, just as Lakshmana said. But Maricha has one last job. With his dying breath he shouts, and the voice that comes out is Rama's. Exactly Rama's, crying out in pain. Oh Sita! Oh Lakshmana! Rama hears it and goes cold. He understands at once, turns, and runs for home. And back at the hut, far away through the trees, Sita hears her husband's voice crying for help.
screen: `THE ARROW HITS.` → `THE DEER BECOMES MARICHA.` → `A DYING SHOUT, IN RAMA'S VOICE.`

segments.voice: Sita turns to Lakshmana: go! He's hurt! Lakshmana doesn't move. Rama told him to guard her, whatever happened, and he knows his brother. Nobody in the three worlds can defeat Rama, he says. That's a trick: the demon, using his voice. I'm staying. Now the scene gets hard. Sita, terrified, says the worst things she can think of. In Valmiki she accuses Lakshmana of wanting Rama dead: that he's secretly after her himself, or working for Bharata. It's cruel, it's unfair, and she's out of her mind with fear. Lakshmana, the brother who gave up everything to follow them, is stung to the core. He tells her he can't bear to hear her say that. And he goes. There are two voices in this scene. One is fake: a demon doing a perfect impression. One is real: a loyal brother saying, calmly, it's not him. The fake one was louder. It had all the right sounds, and it hit exactly where Sita was most afraid. That's how false signals work. They don't sound false. They sound like the person you love, in trouble, right now, and they're built to make you move before you think. The tradition doesn't blame Sita alone, and it doesn't make Lakshmana a fool for going. It shows how fear turns good people against each other in a minute. When something makes you panic, that's the moment to ask who is really speaking. Check the voice.
screen: `GO! HE'S HURT!` · `NOBODY CAN DEFEAT RAMA.` · `FEAR SAYS THE WORST THINGS.` · `THE FAKE VOICE WAS LOUDER.` · then, large: `CHECK THE VOICE.`

segments.voice: Remember a time panic moved you before you checked: a scary message, a rumor, a headline, an alarm that turned out to be nothing, or a time fear made you say something you didn't mean to someone loyal. Hold it without blame, breathe slowly, and imagine what one calm question would have changed.
The cry. Maricha, dying, shouts in Rama's voice, and Sita, terrified, drives Lakshmana away from the hut.
Your line: check the voice. In that scene, Lakshmana's was the quiet one. That's fifty days in.

howItsDone: Hindus retell the scene of the false cry as a warning about deception and fear; in many tellings, and in discussion at home, people weigh Sita's panic and Lakshmana's hurt without blaming either alone.

original.note: Sanskrit: voice, sound, tone; Maricha's dying cry in Rama's voice.

trapdoor: what you thought: Sita was fooled by a trick.
what it means: a perfect fake voice hits where she's most afraid, and fear turns two loyal people against each other.
what a scholar hears: Valmiki gives Sita a harsh accusation of Lakshmana here; many later retellings soften it, and Lakshmana's hurt is part of what drives the plot.
